title: Amazon nears $7.5 billion Decart acquisition, FT reports — deal could close next week
subtitle: The Financial Times says Amazon is in advanced talks to buy the Trainium3-adopter AI startup, with the transaction structured as cash, stock and earnouts and expected as soon as the following week.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Financial Times reported on Saturday that Amazon is in advanced talks to acquire San Francisco–based AI startup Decart for approximately $7.5 billion, with an agreement possible as soon as the following week. The paper says the price is 'more than $7 billion, up to about $7.5 billion with earnouts,' and that the deal would be structured as a mix of cash, stock and deferred consideration — a shape that lines up with what the Israeli outlet Calcalist reported on Tuesday. Amazon and Decart have both declined to comment. Decart was last valued at $4 billion in May, following a $300 million round backed by Sequoia Capital and Nvidia.

Decart builds software that lets developers run AI workloads across chip architectures without rewriting them. The company was an early adopter of AWS's Trainium3, and that is probably the point of the deal. AWS's custom-silicon push — Trainium for training, Inferentia for inference — has always had the same adoption problem: shops that have standardized on CUDA are expensive to peel off. A tooling layer that abstracts across GPUs, Trainium and competing accelerators is a shortcut past that problem, worth paying a premium for if you are AWS.

The timing is also strategic. Google's TPU campaign has had a visible 2026 — Anthropic's expansion onto TPUs in October, and now Anthropic's November 21 claim that Claude Mythos ported a workload to AMD MI355X chips in three days. Both items challenge the assumption that Nvidia's software moat is unbreakable. If Amazon can buy a credible cross-silicon runtime at $7.5 billion, the price looks cheap against the alternative of waiting for the ecosystem to grow organically around Trainium. The risk is the one that haunts every talent-plus-tech acquisition at this scale: the team walks and the roadmap stalls.

A note for learners: the number to watch in acquisitions like this is not the headline price but the earnout structure. When a deal is 'up to $7.5 billion,' the distance between the floor and the ceiling tells you how much the buyer thinks the thesis actually depends on specific people hitting specific milestones. A big earnout is a signal of execution risk, not a signal of generosity. If the final filing shows a small earnout, Amazon is paying for the IP. A large one means they're paying for the team to deliver it.
